questions.stem: The day and night shift supervisors on your food plant's line upgrade have stopped speaking to each other. Everything now passes through the written handover log. Three of the last five late starts trace back to information that sat in someone's head and never reached the log. Asked separately, both supervisors tell you the arrangement is working fine. Your project engineer wants the two shifts merged under one supervisor. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Merge the two shifts under a single supervisor for the remainder of the upgrade, as the project engineer suggests.
options.rationale: A structural change chosen before the cause is known fixes whatever the engineer has guessed at. It also removes one person's role as the price of a disagreement nobody has yet described.

options.text: Meet each supervisor separately to establish what the disagreement is actually about before deciding on any change.
options.rationale: Two people who both say nothing is wrong will say something different in private from what they say together. The source has to be established before any approach to resolving it can be chosen.

options.text: Strengthen the handover log with a mandatory checklist so that nothing important depends on conversation.
options.rationale: It treats the lost information as a documentation defect. The log is where the avoidance is showing, not where it comes from, and a longer form will be completed by two people still not talking.

options.text: Bring both supervisors into a facilitated session immediately and ask them to settle the disagreement between them.
options.rationale: Facilitating before you know what is in dispute puts two people in a room to discover it in front of you. It also risks naming as a conflict something one of them considers closed.

questions.explanation: Withdrawal is a stage of conflict rather than the absence of one, and when two people route everything through a document the cost appears as information that never reaches anybody. The source has to be established before an approach is selected, and the people closest to it usually describe it differently in private from how they describe it together. Any structural remedy chosen first is a remedy for a guess.
questions.mindset: Treat silence between two people who must coordinate as a symptom to be investigated, not as a problem that has gone away.

questions.stem: In a sprint review for a housing association's tenant portal, a resident representative says the new repairs form is confusing. A developer replies that the residents' panel has changed its mind three times and that some people cannot be pleased. The room goes quiet and the product owner looks across at you. Eleven people are on the call, including two of the association's directors. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Say nothing during the session and raise the remark with the developer privately once the call has finished.
options.rationale: The resident and eleven other people saw the exchange and will not see the private conversation. Silence in the moment reads as agreement with the remark.

options.text: Put the exchange on the retrospective agenda so the team can agree how it wants to handle criticism from residents.
options.rationale: It treats the team's process as the injured party when the injured party is sitting in the meeting. A retrospective days later cannot repair something the customer experienced today.

options.text: Step in at once, acknowledge the resident's point, return the session to the form, and speak to the developer later.
options.rationale: Intervening while the audience is still present is what repairs the moment, and it settles nothing about who is right on the form. The private conversation is still owed, just not instead of this.

options.text: Apologise on the team's behalf, end the review early and reschedule the remaining demonstration for a day later in the week.
options.rationale: Ending the session makes one remark into an incident and costs the team its feedback. It also leaves the resident with an apology and no answer about the form.

questions.explanation: Conduct in front of a customer is handled in the moment, because the audience is part of the harm and a private conversation they never see cannot undo it. Stepping in is not a ruling on who is right about the work; it is a statement about what the session is for. Deferring to a later forum protects the team's comfort at the expense of the person who was actually in the room.
questions.mindset: Repair a public exchange in public, at the time, and keep the private conversation as well as it, not instead of it.

questions.stem: Two analysts on your pharmaceutical stability programme have disagreed for three days about which of two testing sequences to run. The argument is technical, public and civil, and each has produced data for their position. Your sponsor, who sits two floors up, tells you to shut it down and pick one so the team can get on. The sequence must be fixed before the next batch is released in a fortnight.

options.text: Choose one of the two sequences yourself today and tell both analysts that the matter is closed.
options.rationale: It spends the project manager's authority on a technical question two better-qualified people are still resolving, and it does so a fortnight before the answer is needed.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to decide between the two sequences, since they are the one who wants it settled quickly.
options.rationale: The sponsor wants the noise to stop, which is not the same as being able to judge the science. Handing them the decision converts an instruction about tone into a technical ruling nobody asked for.

options.text: Let the discussion run its course and revisit it if the fortnight begins to look tight.
options.rationale: A productive argument still needs a mechanism for ending. Leaving the close undefined means the answer eventually gets chosen by whoever tires last or by the batch date.

options.text: Tell the sponsor the debate is productive, then give it a decision date, criteria and a named decider.
options.rationale: The sponsor's concern is that it will not end, which a boundary answers without discarding the evidence the two analysts are generating.

questions.explanation: Disagreement about the work is not the same thing as disagreement between people, and only the second one needs stopping. A technical argument that is producing evidence is the cheapest assurance a project gets. What it needs is a boundary — a date, the criteria it will be judged against and the name of whoever decides if it is still open — so that it converges rather than running until something external forces an answer.
questions.mindset: Before ending an argument, ask whether it is doing work; a disagreement about the work usually needs a deadline rather than a verdict.

questions.stem: An anonymous mid-project survey on your claims transformation returns three separate comments describing a senior data architect as dismissive in reviews. His output is excellent and you have not seen the behaviour yourself. He is assigned to you from the data function and his appraisal is written by its head. Eight people completed the survey, so the three commenters are identifiable to anyone who thinks about it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take the pattern to the head of the data function, who can gather attributable evidence and act on it.
options.rationale: The comments are a signal rather than a case, and the person who can turn one into the other holds the line relationship. Passing it there keeps the response fair to the architect.

options.text: Share the anonymised comments with the architect at your next one-to-one and ask him how he reads them.
options.rationale: In a group of eight the anonymity is nominal, so it exposes the commenters. It also asks him to answer a charge with no instance attached to it, which invites denial rather than change.

options.text: Run a session on the working agreement for how the team gives and takes feedback in reviews, naming nobody.
options.rationale: Using a whole-team session to send a message to one person is read correctly by everyone and acted on by no one. It also spends the team's time on a norm most of them are already keeping.

options.text: Sit in on the next few design reviews yourself and act only on the behaviour you have witnessed there.
options.rationale: It sets a standard of proof that leaves three people who already spoke up carrying the cost, and a person who is careful in front of the project manager will stay careful.

questions.explanation: Feedback that cannot be attributed cannot be actioned as an accusation, but a pattern several people describe is not something a project manager is free to set aside either. The route is to whoever can collect attributable evidence and holds authority over the person's conduct, which on a matrix project is rarely the project manager. Relaying anonymous comments to their subject risks the people who gave them and leaves the subject no fair way to answer.
questions.mindset: Act on unattributable feedback by finding the person who can make it attributable, not by repeating it.

questions.stem: On a telecoms billing migration, a tester has raised four defects at severity two over six weeks and the lead architect has downgraded every one to severity three without discussing it with her. She has now stopped raising anything above severity three. Your severity definitions exist but describe severity two only as significant customer impact. Both are competent, and neither has complained to you about the other.

options.text: Ask the architect to walk the tester through the reasoning behind each of the four downgrades.
options.rationale: It improves the courtesy of a decision the architect will still make alone. The next case arrives with the same undefined term and the same imbalance of standing.

options.text: Restore the four defects to severity two and tell the architect to route future changes through you.
options.rationale: It substitutes the project manager's judgement for a technical one and creates a bottleneck. Reversing the calls without changing the criterion just moves who wins the argument.

options.text: Get the two of them to define severity two in measurable terms and agree who decides a disputed case.
options.rationale: The recurring dispute is about an undefined word, and defining it converts a contest of standing into a test anyone can apply.

options.text: Raise it as a quality risk with the sponsor and ask for an independent review of the defect log.
options.rationale: It escalates a disagreement that has never been put to either party, and an external review of the log will reach the same ambiguity in the definitions.

questions.explanation: Repeated disagreement about the same judgement usually means the criterion is undefined rather than that one party is wrong. Where a rule leaves the decisive term to interpretation, the argument returns with every case and the person with more standing wins by default; the visible effect is the junior party raising less, which removes the signal rather than the disagreement. Define the term, then name who resolves it when it is still contested.
questions.mindset: When the same argument keeps recurring, suspect the definition before you suspect the people.

questions.stem: Your London editorial team says the Manila production team does not care, citing three queries sent late in the afternoon and answered only the next day. Manila's lead says London sends incomplete briefs and then chases them. The two locations share three hours of working day. A senior London editor has asked you to insist on same-day answers as a standard. Both leads are respected by their own teams.

options.text: Plot when queries are sent against the shared hours, and take what that shows to both teams.
options.rationale: It replaces two accounts of each other's character with one account of the working day, which both sides can check and neither can dismiss.

options.text: Agree a same-day response commitment with the Manila team and review how it holds over two sprints.
options.rationale: It writes one side's complaint into a standard before testing whether the standard is achievable in three shared hours, and makes the other team the only one under measurement.

options.text: Ask the two leads to hold a call to clear the air about how each team sees the other.
options.rationale: It treats a structural problem as a relationship problem. Two leads can part on good terms and the afternoon queries will still arrive after Manila has gone home.

options.text: Introduce a brief template so that every query carries the information Manila says is missing.
options.rationale: It adopts the second team's explanation as the cause without checking it. The template may well be useful, but choosing it now means one account has been believed and the other has not.

questions.explanation: Attributing a pattern to somebody's attitude is a conclusion, and it is usually reached before anyone has looked at when things actually happen. Distributed work fails on overlap, handover quality and the shape of the working day far more often than on goodwill, and all three are measurable. Putting the measurement in front of both parties turns an accusation into a problem they can work on together, and it stops a remedy being built from the loudest account.
questions.mindset: When a team's behaviour is explained by its character, look first for the constraint that would produce the same behaviour in anyone.

questions.stem: Your collections system supplier is six weeks late on two deliverables, and you have been managing it through the contract's monthly review. The supplier's account director has now invited your sponsor to lunch to, in his words, reset the relationship. Your sponsor forwards the invitation and asks whether she should accept. The next contract review is in nine days and you hold the delegated authority for the contract.

options.text: Encourage the sponsor to accept the invitation, and brief her thoroughly on the delivery record the day before.
options.rationale: A good briefing does not change where the conversation happens. It concedes that late delivery is discussed above the project manager, and the next slip will go the same way.

options.text: Ask to attend the lunch yourself as well, so that the delivery position is represented accurately there.
options.rationale: Attending legitimises the venue. The supplier still achieves the thing it wanted, which is the sponsor in the room for a discussion the contract puts elsewhere.

options.text: Send the supplier a formal notice about the late deliverables before any meeting takes place.
options.rationale: It jumps past a review mechanism that has not yet been used for this slip, hardening positions over a delay that may still be recoverable through the normal route.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to decline and to point the account director at the contract's review meeting.
options.rationale: It puts the discussion back where both parties agreed it would happen, and it does so without treating the approach as bad faith.

questions.explanation: A dispute about a project raised outside the project's own machinery is an attempt, deliberate or not, to move a decision to someone with less information about it. Redirecting it to the agreed forum is not defensiveness; it is what keeps a governance or contract route meaningful, and it preserves senior attention for the things only that level can settle. Accepting the invitation concedes the principle however good the briefing is.
questions.mindset: Answer an approach that goes over your head by using the authority you hold, not by preparing the person it went to.

questions.stem: Your university's student records replacement has had the same argument three times in two months: whether departments may keep their own local spreadsheets after go-live. A decision was taken in July that they may not, but it was made in a meeting of four people and never written down anywhere. Two departments are now building their cutover plans as though nothing had been settled.

options.text: Hold a fourth session and let the two departments make their case properly this time.
options.rationale: It reopens a question that was decided, which teaches every department that persistence is the way to get a second hearing on anything it dislikes.

options.text: Publish the July decision and its reasoning in the decision log, and confirm it to both departments.
options.rationale: A decision only exists for people who were not in the room once it is written down with its reasoning, which also gives anyone who disagrees something specific to challenge.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to send a message reminding everyone that local spreadsheets are not permitted.
options.rationale: It borrows authority to cover a gap in the record. The message settles this month and leaves no durable trace, so the argument returns with the next planning round.

options.text: Add the local spreadsheet question to the risk register and monitor whether it causes a problem at cutover.
options.rationale: It converts a settled decision back into an open uncertainty. Monitoring is the right response to something that might happen, not to something that was agreed and not communicated.

questions.explanation: An argument that recurs on the same question usually means the decision was never made visible, not that people are being difficult. Until a decision is recorded with its reasoning and communicated, planning around it is rational rather than defiant. Reopening the debate rewards the gap in the record; closing the gap ends the argument and gives dissenters a clear thing to contest if they still want to.
questions.mindset: A decision that is not written down has not been made for anyone who was not in the room.

questions.stem: Two product owners at a grocery retailer have each told your platform squad that their request is the top priority for the coming sprint, and each has a launch date behind it. The developers have asked you, as delivery manager, to tell them which one to build first. The two product owners report to the same director and sprint planning is tomorrow morning.

options.text: Decide on the squad's behalf, using the two launch dates as the tiebreaker between the requests.
options.rationale: It relieves the pressure by taking a decision about business value that belongs to the people accountable for it, and a launch date is not by itself a measure of worth.

options.text: Have the squad start both and see which is further along at the midpoint of the sprint.
options.rationale: Splitting the team across both defers the choice and makes it more likely neither finishes. It also hides the conflict inside the sprint instead of settling it before planning.

options.text: Get the two product owners to produce one ranked list together before the sprint is planned.
options.rationale: One list forces the trade-off to be made by the people who own the value, and it leaves a record of what was chosen over what.

options.text: Ask their director to rank the two items so that the squad has an instruction to work to.
options.rationale: It escalates past two people who have the information and the standing to decide, and it trains them to route future disagreements upwards rather than to each other.

questions.explanation: Two people claiming the same priority have a prioritisation problem, and a delivery team cannot solve it without assuming a decision that is not theirs. Making the owners produce a single ranked list puts the trade-off with the people accountable for the value and records what was set aside. Deciding on their behalf removes the pressure and the accountability at the same time, and escalating removes it from people who could have exercised it.
questions.mindset: Give a decision back to whoever owns its consequences, especially when they are asking you to take it.

questions.stem: A month ago you moved two testers from the ticketing workstream to the terminals workstream on your ferry operator's programme. The two workstream leads have been in open dispute about test coverage ever since. The ticketing lead tells you privately that you caused the problem and that she will not accept you chairing a session to resolve it. You still believe the reallocation was the right call.

options.text: Ask a colleague from outside the programme to facilitate the session, and attend it as a party.
options.rationale: It accepts that impartiality is judged by the parties, and it lets the reallocation be defended on its merits by the person who made it.

options.text: Chair the session as planned and open it by setting out the reasoning behind the reallocation of the testers.
options.rationale: It overrides a stated objection to your neutrality, so every outcome will look like self-justification however sound the original decision was.

options.text: Reverse the reallocation to remove the cause, then let the two leads settle the coverage question.
options.rationale: It unmakes a decision you still think correct in order to buy quiet, and it shows that objecting loudly enough is how resourcing gets changed.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to chair the session, since the reallocation was a programme-level decision.
options.rationale: It turns a workstream dispute into a hearing on the project manager's judgement in front of the sponsor, which is a heavier remedy than the disagreement needs.

questions.explanation: Impartiality is judged by the parties, not asserted by the person claiming it. Once your own decision is part of what is in dispute you are a party to it, and chairing makes any outcome look like self-justification. Handing the chair to someone neutral lets the decision be argued on its merits and lets you make that argument. Undoing a sound decision to remove friction buys quiet at the price of the plan.
questions.mindset: You cannot mediate a conflict your own decision created; find a chair and argue your case as a party.

questions.stem: Six weeks after your company acquired a soil-sensor firm, the two engineering groups work as one squad. The acquired engineers merge to trunk several times a day; the original group works on branches that are reviewed for two days. Each side calls the other's practice reckless or slow, and both have shipped reliably for years. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Have the squad agree one working definition of done for the merged codebase, with both practices on the table.
options.rationale: One codebase can only carry one standard, and building it in the open is what makes it survive the first time somebody is inconvenienced by it.

options.text: Adopt the practice of the acquiring company's group, since it is the standard the organisation already runs to.
options.rationale: It settles the question by ownership rather than by reasoning, and it discards whatever risk the other practice was managing without anyone naming what that was.

options.text: Let each group keep its own practice on the parts of the codebase it knows best for the time being.
options.rationale: It preserves the split it was meant to resolve and adds a second problem, because the boundary between the two halves of the codebase now needs policing too.

options.text: Ask each group to state what its practice protects against, before any decision about which to keep.
options.rationale: Stated risks can be compared, whereas adjectives like reckless and slow cannot, and it moves the argument off character within one conversation.

options.text: Bring in an external engineering consultant to recommend which practice the merged squad should adopt.
options.rationale: It outsources a decision the squad has to live with, and a recommendation nobody in the room owns is the easiest thing in the world to quietly ignore.

questions.explanation: Two established practices in conflict are usually two different risk models, and the argument stays about character until each side says what its practice protects against. A merged team needs one standard because the artefact is one artefact, and a standard assembled from both sets of reasons holds better than one inherited from the stronger party. Deciding by seniority or by consultant leaves the losing practice's risk unmanaged and unnamed.
questions.mindset: Ask what a practice is protecting against before judging whether it is worth keeping.

questions.stem: In March you brokered a written agreement between the commissioning manager and the marine coordinator on your offshore wind project: vessel requests go in ten days ahead, and confirmations come back within two. It is now May. Two of the last four requests went in at four days' notice and one confirmation took nine days. Neither of them has raised it with you or with each other. The next quarterly review is six weeks away.

options.text: Wait for the quarterly review in six weeks, where the pattern can be raised with both of their managers present.
options.rationale: Six weeks turns four specific instances into a general complaint, which is easier to deny and harder to act on than a request that went in on a named date.

options.text: Rewrite the agreement with shorter notice periods that match what the two of them are actually doing.
options.rationale: It adopts the breach as the standard before anyone has said why the original was unworkable, which may simply be untrue of the nine-day confirmation.

options.text: Track the next month of requests and confirmations so that you have a fuller picture before raising it with them.
options.rationale: The evidence needed is already in hand. More data here is delay with a rigorous justification attached, and it lets the pattern set for another month.

options.text: Put the four requests in front of both of them this week and ask what is stopping the agreement working.
options.rationale: It raises the breach while specific instances are still available to discuss, and it opens the possibility that the terms were wrong rather than ignored.

questions.explanation: An agreement is worth what is done when it is broken, and the moment to raise a breach is while a specific instance can still be pointed at. Waiting for a scheduled forum converts particular facts into a general grievance. Rewriting the standard to match the behaviour is a decision to have no standard. Asking what is stopping it working matters because most broken agreements turn out to have been unworkable rather than ignored.
questions.mindset: Raise a breach while it still has a date attached to it, and ask why before you ask who.

questions.stem: Your waste fleet telematics rollout lost one of its three integration engineers to long-term sickness eight weeks ago, and you spread her work across the other two. Both have hit every date since. One has now told you the other is coasting, and the pair avoid each other in stand-ups. The sponsor has not been told the team is at two-thirds strength. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the two engineers to agree between themselves a fairer split of the work left behind by their colleague.
options.rationale: It makes two people under pressure arbitrate a shortage neither of them created, and whatever split they reach leaves the same total load on the same two people.

options.text: Put the plan, the two engineers and yourself in one room to decide what is dropped or deferred.
options.rationale: The overload is the thing generating the resentment, and it can only be reduced by a decision about the work rather than about how the work is divided.

options.text: Speak to the engineer who used the word coasting about how that comment lands on a colleague.
options.rationale: It corrects the expression of the grievance and leaves the grievance itself untouched, which usually drives the complaint underground rather than resolving it.

options.text: Hold the current dates and revisit the workload once the absent engineer's return is confirmed.
options.rationale: It asks two people to endure an indefinite overload on the strength of a date nobody controls, and long-term sickness rarely has a return date worth planning against.

options.text: Tell the sponsor the team is at two-thirds capacity and what that costs on the current dates.
options.rationale: The sponsor is making commitments on dates that are only being met by absorption, and only they can decide whether to buy capacity or move a date.

questions.explanation: Absorbing the loss of a resource without changing the plan moves the conflict into the team, where it surfaces as resentment between the people carrying the load. Two things are owed: a decision about what will not be done, and an honest statement of capacity to whoever is relying on the dates. Asking the people under pressure to divide the shortfall between them delegates a planning decision to the two individuals least able to make it.
questions.mindset: When a team starts turning on itself, look at what the plan is asking of it before you look at the people.

questions.stem: Nine days before a medical device submission, two of your four reviewers are disputing who was responsible for a literature search that was missed last quarter. Both are working the submission and the output has not suffered. Resolving it properly needs a facilitated session and probably a conversation with their head of department, who is on leave until the day before filing. Neither has asked you to intervene.

options.text: Hold a short facilitated session with both reviewers this week so the dispute does not surface during the final review.
options.rationale: It spends scarce reviewer attention on an accountability question that cannot be settled without the head of department, and half-finished mediation tends to inflame rather than settle.

options.text: Tell both of them you are parking it until the submission is filed, and set the date now.
options.rationale: Naming the date is what makes this a decision rather than an omission, and it stops either party reading your silence as a judgement on the merits.

options.text: Deal with it informally by speaking to each of them separately over the next few days.
options.rationale: Informal handling of a question about accountability produces two private accounts and no shared conclusion, and it consumes the same days as the formal route.

options.text: Leave it alone and see whether it still matters once the submission pressure has lifted.
options.rationale: It reaches the same nine days of quiet without anyone owning what happens afterwards, so the issue depends on someone raising it again from a standing start.

questions.explanation: Deferring a conflict is a legitimate choice when the cost of resolving it now exceeds the cost of carrying it, and what separates deferral from avoidance is that a deferral has a date and both parties have been told. Naming the date keeps the issue owned, stops either party concluding it has been dismissed, and lets the immediate work have the attention it needs. The test is not whether a conflict is being left, but whether anyone is accountable for returning to it.
questions.mindset: Parking a conflict is a decision only if it has a date and both parties have heard it.

questions.stem: The clinical lead at a regional hospital will release the imaging room only at weekends. The estates manager will only supply contractors on weekdays, because weekend rates break his budget. Each has told you the other is being unreasonable, and each cites the other's refusal as the reason the installation has not started. The work needs nine consecutive days. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Book the weekday slots the estates manager offers and tell the clinical lead the dates are fixed.
options.rationale: It resolves the conflict by choosing a side, and the side it chooses cannot deliver the room. The installation would arrive to find the space in clinical use.

options.text: Ask your sponsor to instruct the two of them to reach an agreement by the end of the week.
options.rationale: An instruction to agree adds pressure without adding information, and neither party can concede a constraint that belongs to their own budget or service.

options.text: Put both constraints and the nine-day requirement into one schedule the two can look at together.
options.rationale: Laid out together, the two constraints stop being evidence of unreasonableness and become a visible gap that no amount of goodwill closes.

options.text: Split the installation into weekday and weekend phases so that each party gets part of what they want.
options.rationale: It divides the difference on a requirement that cannot be divided. Nine consecutive days is a technical constraint, not an opening position in a negotiation.

options.text: Cost the weekend premium and take it to whoever can authorise it as a funding decision.
options.rationale: Once the gap is visible the remaining question is money, and that belongs to someone with a budget rather than to two people defending theirs.

questions.explanation: When two parties each hold a constraint the other cannot satisfy, the disagreement is not about reasonableness and will not yield to persuasion. Setting both constraints against the actual requirement shows whether any solution exists, and where none does, the conflict resolves into a decision somebody has to fund or authorise. Splitting the difference is only a resolution where the requirement itself can be split, which is exactly what the nine consecutive days decide here.
questions.mindset: Put two incompatible constraints side by side before judging either party, because the gap is usually a decision rather than an attitude.

questions.stem: In one week on a brewery's direct-to-consumer squad you handled three disagreements differently. On Monday a checkout defect was losing orders, two developers disagreed about the fix, and you chose one and said the decision stood until Friday. On Wednesday you accepted the designer's preferred button colour, a point you did not care about, to keep goodwill for later. On Thursday you spent two hours with both leads until the question of who owns the payments service had an answer each of them could support. Name the approach used on each day.

blanks.label: The approach used on Monday
blanks.rationale: Deciding for the parties and closing the question is forcing, and it is the right choice when orders are being lost and there is no time to build agreement.

blanks.label: The approach used on Wednesday
blanks.rationale: Conceding a point you do not value in order to preserve the relationship is accommodating, and on a matter of taste it costs the project nothing to do so.

blanks.label: The approach used on Thursday
blanks.rationale: Working a question through until both parties can support the outcome is collaborating, which is the only approach that reliably stops an ownership dispute returning.

questions.explanation: No single approach to a disagreement is correct in itself; the choice follows the stakes, the time available and how much the working relationship has to carry afterwards. High stakes with no time argues for deciding and saying so; a point you do not care about is worth conceding cheaply, because goodwill spent well is an asset; and a question that will otherwise keep returning deserves the hours it takes to find an answer both parties can live with. Using one approach for everything is the actual error.
questions.mindset: Choose how to handle a disagreement from what the situation can afford, not from the way you prefer to handle disagreements.

questions.stem: A live data-protection incident on your energy retailer's customer app has sent a batch of statements to the wrong addresses. Two engineers disagree about whether to take the statement service down. The next batch runs in thirty minutes and you hold the delegated authority to stop the service. The grid plots concern for your own outcome against concern for the other party's outcome. Select the region showing the approach to take now.

graphic.title: Conflict-handling grid: concern for own outcome against concern for the other party's outcome
graphic.caption: Select a region. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between regions, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: High concern for your outcome, low concern for theirs
regions.rationale: Pressing for the outcome is the fitting approach when harm is accumulating, the decision rights are already yours and there is no time to build agreement before the next batch runs.

regions.label: High concern for both outcomes
regions.rationale: Working to satisfy both positions fully is the best approach when time allows, and it is precisely the time that thirty minutes and a running batch do not give you.

regions.label: Low concern for your outcome, high concern for theirs
regions.rationale: Giving way is a cheap way to keep goodwill on a question you do not care about. A live incident with statements going to the wrong people is not such a question.

regions.label: Low concern for either outcome
regions.rationale: Stepping away suits a dispute that will settle itself or that is not yours to settle. Here the next batch will run whether or not anyone decides, so withdrawing is itself a decision.

regions.label: Partial satisfaction of both outcomes
regions.rationale: Settling on a partial outcome works where positions can be traded against each other. Whether to stop a service is binary, so there is no halfway position to reach for.

questions.explanation: The approach to a disagreement is read from the situation rather than chosen from a preference for being collaborative. Where harm is accumulating, the decision rights already sit with you and there is no time to build agreement, using the authority you hold is the fitting approach, and explaining the reasoning afterwards is part of using it well. What makes this uncomfortable is that the same approach applied where there was time would cost the working relationship for no gain.
questions.mindset: Authority is for the moments when time has run out, and using it then is not a failure of collaboration.

questions.stem: One dispute between the field crews and the data team ran right through your smart metering rollout. Match each point in its life to the intervention that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Month one: crews mention in passing that the tablet's reading screen slows them down, and the data team has not heard this from anyone.
Month three: crews are recording readings on paper and keying them in later, and the data team says the resulting file is full of errors.
Month six: both leads have written to your sponsor, each accusing the other of misrepresenting what happened.

options.text: Get the two teams in front of the same screen so the complaint becomes a specific, testable request.
options.rationale: An early complaint is information that has not reached the people who could act on it, and the cheapest intervention is to close that gap while it is still a remark rather than a position.

options.text: Ask each lead to bring concerns to you privately and keep the two teams apart until tempers cool.
options.rationale: Not used. Routing everything through the project manager is what allows a first complaint to go unheard, and separating teams that depend on each other suppresses the signal rather than the disagreement.

options.text: Measure the error rate and the time the screen costs, and settle the workaround on those numbers.
options.rationale: Both sides now have a real cost and a workaround defending it. Numbers let the two costs be compared, which is what an argument between two reasonable positions needs.

options.text: Convene a formal session with the sponsor present and an agreed written record of what is settled.
options.rationale: Once positions are public and in writing to a sponsor, an informal conversation cannot deliver a resolution either lead can be seen to accept. The record is the point of the setting.

questions.explanation: Conflicts escalate through stages, and each stage takes a different intervention, which is why the same dispute is cheap in month one and formal in month six. Early on it is a piece of information that has not travelled; in the middle it is two workarounds with measurable costs on either side; late on the positions are public and need a setting that produces a record. Reading the stage first is what avoids both over-reacting to a grumble and under-reacting to a breach.
questions.mindset: Match the weight of the intervention to the stage the conflict has reached, because the same remedy is wasteful early and useless late.

questions.stem: A dispute over who signs off master data at a textile manufacturer has held your ERP cutover for a fortnight. Match each party to what they should do next. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: You, the project manager, holding the cutover plan and a fortnight of slippage against it.
The sponsor, who chairs the steering group that approved the data governance model.
The two site operations managers, each of whom has signed off master data for their own site for years.

options.text: Ask the software vendor which role its standard model expects to hold the sign-off.
options.rationale: Not used. A vendor's default configuration describes how the product is usually deployed, not who is accountable in this organisation, and treating it as an answer imports someone else's governance.

options.text: Set out the decision that is needed, the options for it, and what each further week of delay costs.
options.rationale: Framing the question and pricing the delay is the project manager's contribution, and it is what turns a stalemate into something a decision-maker can act on.

options.text: Rule on which role holds the sign-off, since the governance model belongs to the steering group.
options.rationale: Interpreting the accountability model is the sponsor's to do, and a ruling from the body that set it is the only outcome both managers can accept without losing face.

options.text: State the risk each of them carries under either answer, then accept the ruling once it is made.
options.rationale: The parties owe their reasoning to whoever decides and their acceptance to the decision, and a dispute reopened after a ruling is a different and more serious problem.

questions.explanation: Resolving a stalled dispute is a division of labour rather than a single act. The project manager frames the decision and its cost, the sponsor rules where the accountability model is theirs to interpret, and the parties put their risk on the table and then live with the answer. Conflicts stall when one of those parts is missing, most often when the situation is described as a disagreement between people rather than as a question somebody has the standing to settle.
questions.mindset: Ask who has the standing to answer a question before trying to get two people to agree on it.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two engineers on your car-sharing app argue every fortnight about who covers the on-call rota, and nobody has ever been told whose job it is to set it. The source here is best described as
A third engineer will not hand her build scripts to the new joiner, having decided he was hired to take over her work. The source here is best described as

options.text: an unclear role boundary, which will keep producing the argument until somebody defines it
options.rationale: Where nobody owns a recurring task, each round of the argument starts from the same undefined position, so the dispute is a property of the gap rather than of the two people in it.

options.text: a perceived threat to standing, which no amount of process clarity will settle on its own
options.rationale: The withheld scripts are protecting a position, not a boundary. Clarifying the handover only confirms the fear unless somebody addresses what she believes it means for her.

options.text: a difference of technical opinion, which sharpens a decision rather than obstructing it
options.rationale: Not used. Neither situation turns on a judgement about how the work should be done; one is about who decides and the other is about what the change means for a person.

questions.explanation: Naming the source of a conflict determines whether a process change will help at all. A dispute that exists because nobody owns something disappears once ownership is assigned, whereas a dispute rooted in how someone sees their own standing is untouched by clearer processes and can be worsened by them if the change reads as confirmation of the fear. The first question is what the disagreement is about, not how strongly it is being expressed.
questions.mindset: Name what a conflict is about before choosing a remedy, because process fixes only cure process causes.

questions.stem: You took over a campus energy retrofit six weeks ago. The estates director will not sign the design freeze because, he says, your predecessor promised new heating controls in all eleven buildings; the approved scope covers six. There is no record of any such promise and your predecessor has left the organisation. Until now he has been one of your most supportive stakeholders.

options.text: Add the five remaining buildings to the scope, on the basis that the commitment was made on the project's behalf.
options.rationale: It treats an unrecorded conversation as a baseline change and commits money the sponsor has not agreed. Every other stakeholder now knows how to get scope added.

options.text: Tell the director that the approved scope governs the project and ask him to sign the freeze this week.
options.rationale: It is correct about the document and answers nothing he has raised. A supportive stakeholder who believes he was promised something hears a refusal to engage with it.

options.text: Acknowledge what he was told, then put the five buildings to the sponsor as a scope decision with costs.
options.rationale: It separates the two halves of the problem, so the expectation is taken seriously by you and the money is decided by whoever owns the baseline.

options.text: Ask the director to produce evidence of the promise before the project considers changing anything at all.
options.rationale: It demands proof of a conversation nobody minuted and turns a supportive stakeholder into a claimant defending his own honesty.

questions.explanation: A commitment you did not make and cannot verify is still entirely real to the person who heard it, and the conflict runs on the gap between the expectation and the baseline. Neither honouring nor denying an undocumented promise resolves it: the expectation is acknowledged by the project manager, and the scope question is put to whoever holds the authority to answer it. Handovers leave these gaps as a matter of course.
questions.mindset: Treat an undocumented promise as a real expectation and an unapproved scope item at the same time.

questions.stem: A disagreement between your UX lead and your API lead about who owns error message wording has been running on an email thread since yesterday. Fourteen people are copied, including the client's delivery manager, and the last two replies have been about who said what in a March workshop. The two of them have not spoken directly at any point. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take it off the thread: get the two of them onto a call today and let the email conversation stop.
options.rationale: The thread is supplying an audience and a written record of point-scoring, and neither helps. A direct conversation is the cheapest intervention available today.

options.text: Reply to the thread with a short summary of both positions, so that everyone copied is working from the same picture.
options.rationale: It legitimises the thread as the venue and gives the fourteen spectators another instalment, which makes the disagreement harder for either of them to drop.

options.text: Ask the client's delivery manager whether she has a view on where error message wording should sit.
options.rationale: It draws the customer into an internal ownership dispute and invites her to arbitrate something that is not hers to settle.

options.text: Wait for the thread to run out of energy, and then raise the question of ownership at the next planning session.
options.rationale: Waiting leaves the exchange in front of the client for several more days, and the March argument will have hardened by the time planning comes round.

questions.explanation: Written channels with a wide distribution turn a small disagreement into a performance, because every reply is composed for the people copied rather than for the other party. Moving the conversation to the smallest channel that can carry it removes the audience, and the audience is usually what is keeping it going. The ownership question still has to be settled, but it will not be settled on the thread.
questions.mindset: Move a disagreement to the smallest room that can hold it.

questions.stem: The head of underwriting agrees in every design workshop and then, within days, tells his team the new process will not work and briefs your sponsor in the same terms. He has done this three times. His written feedback is consistently supportive. Your business analyst wants him dropped from the workshops. The next design decision is due in two weeks.

options.text: Drop him from the workshops and take his input in writing, where his position has at least been consistent.
options.rationale: It removes the one forum in which the objection might surface, and it converts a stakeholder who is already briefing against the design into an excluded one.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to tell him that decisions taken in the design workshops are binding on his area.
options.rationale: It enforces compliance with a decision he has never been able to argue against, which buys silence in the workshop and more briefing outside it.

options.text: Record decisions at the end of each workshop and have every attendee confirm their agreement in the room.
options.rationale: It hardens the record of a consent that is not real. He will confirm as he always does, and the conversations afterwards will continue unchanged.

options.text: Meet him privately and ask what he cannot say in the workshop that he is saying afterwards.
options.rationale: Agreement inside a room and dissent outside it points at the room, and asking directly is the only way to find out what the setting is preventing.

questions.explanation: When someone's stated agreement and their behaviour diverge repeatedly, the usual cause is a forum that cannot carry their objection — because of who is present, what it would cost them to say it, or how the decision is framed — rather than dishonesty. Tightening the record of consent captures the symptom more precisely and changes nothing. The diagnosis has to happen somewhere the objection can safely be spoken.
questions.mindset: When agreement and behaviour diverge, suspect the forum before you suspect the person.

questions.stem: Two subcontractors on your distribution centre fit-out are in open dispute. The mechanical firm says the electrical firm leaves cable waste that blocks its work; the electrical firm says it cannot reach its runs until the mechanical plant is moved. Each has written asking you to instruct the other. Both contracts place a coordination duty on each party. Handover is four weeks away.

options.text: Instruct the electrical firm to clear its waste daily, since that is the part of the complaint you can verify.
options.rationale: Instructing on the half you can see settles nothing about the sequence, and it tells the mechanical firm that whoever documents best will win the next round.

options.text: Run a coordination meeting under both contracts and have the two agree a sequence and a clean-up standard.
options.rationale: The obligation to coordinate is already theirs, and the sequence is the thing in dispute, so the meeting produces the one output neither firm can produce alone.

options.text: Issue a compensation event to whichever firm the programme shows to have caused the other's delay.
options.rationale: It converts a coordination failure into a commercial claim with four weeks left, and the two firms will spend those weeks building records rather than working.

options.text: Raise the dispute with both firms' commercial managers so that it is settled above the two site teams.
options.rationale: The only people who can resequence the work are on site. Escalating puts the decision with managers who will ask their site teams what to do.

questions.explanation: Where an obligation to coordinate already exists, the project manager's job is to convene it rather than to adjudicate between the parties, because an instruction to one of them takes a side in a dispute that is about the order of two workstreams. Turning a coordination failure into a claim moves the conflict into a process built for attributing blame after the event, which is the wrong machinery when the work is still live.
questions.mindset: When a duty to coordinate already exists, call it in rather than deciding for the parties.

questions.stem: Two developers on a squad have been sniping at each other in stand-ups. Their team lead told you a fortnight ago that she was dealing with it and asked you to leave it with her. This morning one of the developers told you directly that nothing has changed and that he wants you to step in. Delivery has not been affected so far.

options.text: Go back to the team lead, tell her what you have been told, and ask what support she needs.
options.rationale: It keeps the problem with the person who owns it while giving her the information she is missing, and it treats her lack of progress as a question rather than a verdict.

options.text: Speak to both developers yourself, now that one of them has asked you directly to get involved.
options.rationale: It takes the problem off the lead without telling her, which undercuts her with her own team and teaches the squad to bypass her when she is slow.

options.text: Tell the developer this is his team lead's to handle and that he should raise it with her again.
options.rationale: It is accurate about the route and leaves the information with nobody who will act on it, after he has already taken a risk in raising it with you.

options.text: Watch the next few stand-ups and step in only if the behaviour starts to affect the squad's delivery.
options.rationale: It makes damage to the work the threshold for acting on how people are treated, by which point the conflict is considerably more expensive to resolve.

questions.explanation: Delegating a problem does not mean losing interest in it, and new information about a delegated problem goes to the person holding it rather than around them. Supporting someone who is struggling with a conflict keeps both the ownership and the relationship intact, while stepping over them resolves this instance and weakens their standing for every future one. The person who raised it is owed an answer about what happens next, not a redirection.
questions.mindset: Give new information to the person who owns the problem, rather than taking the problem off them.

questions.stem: Your data migration lead told the steering group that a three-week slip was caused by the client delivering files late. You have since seen an email chain showing the files arrived on the agreed date and that his own team had not finished the mapping. The client's programme manager is drafting a formal response to the accusation. The lead has worked for you for two years.

options.text: Correct the record with the steering group yourself and let the lead account for the attribution there.
options.rationale: It settles the record at the cost of making him answer in front of the group, and it commits you to an account of events you have not yet tested with him.

options.text: Tell the client's programme manager privately that the attribution was wrong, before her response goes out.
options.rationale: It repairs the external damage first and goes around your own lead to do it, which is how you find out later that there was a version of events you had not heard.

options.text: Ask your sponsor how she would like a misstatement to the steering group to be handled in this case.
options.rationale: It escalates a matter you have not established, and describing it as a misstatement to the sponsor has already reached the conclusion the conversation should test.

options.text: Put the email chain in front of the lead today and ask him to account for the discrepancy.
options.rationale: Everything that follows depends on whether this was an error or a misstatement, and the only person who can tell you that has not yet been asked.

questions.explanation: Evidence that looks conclusive still does not tell you what happened, and the distinction between a mistake and a deliberate misattribution determines whether the response is a correction, a conversation or something more serious. Going to the person first is not delay: it is what makes the correction accurate, and the external record cannot be put right until you know what is actually being corrected. Two years of working relationship is a reason to ask, not a reason to assume.
questions.mindset: Ask the person before you act on the evidence, because the account changes what the evidence means.

questions.stem: Your head of service operations will not accept the new payments module into support: he says his team has no capacity for it and that nobody asked him. Your product owner says the release date is fixed and that support is an operations matter. The module goes live in three weeks, and the two of them have stopped attending each other's meetings.

options.text: Release on the agreed date and log the support gap as an issue for operations to resolve afterwards.
options.rationale: It ships a known gap and moves the conflict into live service, where it will be argued over incidents affecting customers rather than over a plan.

options.text: Quantify the support load the module adds and put it into the release decision as a cost.
options.rationale: A capacity claim and a fixed date are both assertions until the load is sized, and sizing it turns the standoff into a decision someone can actually take.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to direct operations to accept the module on the agreed release date.
options.rationale: It compels acceptance of a capacity claim nobody has tested, so either the claim was true and service suffers, or it was untrue and nobody ever found out.

options.text: Delay the release until operations confirms that it has recruited the capacity it says it needs.
options.rationale: It accepts an unquantified claim as a hard constraint and hands one party an indefinite veto over the release date.

questions.explanation: A dispute between two parties who each hold an unexamined assertion cannot be resolved by choosing one of them, and the readiness of an operation to receive something is a measurable quantity rather than an opinion. Making the cost visible converts a disagreement about whose priority wins into a decision about what the organisation is willing to pay, which is a decision that has an owner. Handover capacity is part of the release, not a consequence of it.
questions.mindset: Size the thing being argued about, because most standoffs are two assertions that nobody has priced.

questions.stem: Three weeks ago your squad decided, after a long discussion, to standardise on a single shared component library. One developer argued against it, lost the argument and has raised it again in each of the last two refinement sessions with the same points. Nothing new has emerged. The rest of the squad has started to disengage whenever he begins.

options.text: Let him make the case once more, properly, so that he can see the decision was fairly taken.
options.rationale: He has already made it at length and lost; a third hearing of unchanged arguments costs the squad another session and confirms that persistence buys airtime.

options.text: Ask him to stop raising the library question in refinement and to bring his concerns to you instead.
options.rationale: It routes dissent privately through the project manager, which removes it from the squad's view and teaches everyone that disagreement is handled offstage.

options.text: Remind the squad the decision stands until new evidence appears, and ask him what evidence would change it.
options.rationale: It keeps the decision stable while leaving a legitimate route to reopen it, and it asks him for the one thing that would justify doing so.

options.text: Put the decision back on the agenda for the next retrospective so that the squad can revisit it properly.
options.rationale: Reopening on persistence rather than on evidence means no decision this squad takes is ever safe from the person least willing to let it go.

questions.explanation: A decision taken after genuine disagreement holds only if the condition for reopening it is stated and is something other than repetition. Naming new evidence as that condition preserves the dissenter's standing to raise it again while protecting the team from relitigating settled questions, and it usually ends the matter, because the person who cannot name what would change their mind has learned something about their own position.
questions.mindset: Decisions reopen on new evidence, not on repetition; say so, and ask what that evidence would be.

questions.stem: Residents on two streets have formed a group objecting to your water main replacement, and their councillor has asked for the works to stop. Daytime working would close the only vehicle access to a primary school; night working is exactly what the residents are objecting to. The scheme has eleven weeks to run and both patterns are permitted under your consent.

options.text: Offer the group a shorter nightly working window in exchange for a longer overall programme.
options.rationale: Duration and intensity are the two things the residents actually weigh against each other, and trading one for the other is available without touching the school access.

options.text: Move to daytime working and manage the school access through a temporary traffic plan instead.
options.rationale: It buys peace with one group by creating a safety problem for another, and the school has less capacity to absorb it than the streets do.

options.text: Explain to the councillor that the consent permits night working and that the programme will continue.
options.rationale: It answers an objection with an entitlement. Being permitted to do something is not an argument that it should be done in this way for eleven weeks.

options.text: Pause the works while the group's objections are considered again by the consenting authority.
options.rationale: It reopens a decision the authority has already taken, at a cost to the programme, and raises an expectation the reconsideration will not meet.

questions.explanation: Where a constraint cannot be removed, the negotiable dimensions are usually intensity and duration, and an objecting party will often accept more weeks of less disruption. Finding that trade requires knowing what the other side is actually protecting, which is rarely identical to the demand they opened with. Relying on the permission you hold wins the legal point and leaves you delivering eleven weeks of work against organised opposition.
questions.mindset: When you cannot remove a disruption, look for what the other party will trade it against.

questions.stem: You are chairing a steering group when the finance director and the operations director begin arguing about whether the pilot site should be Leeds or Derby. Within a minute the exchange has moved to a disagreement from a previous programme. Six other people are waiting, and the pilot site is the only item that must be settled today.

options.text: Let the exchange run, since two directors are entitled to settle their differences in their own forum.
options.rationale: The chair's job is the meeting's purpose, and leaving it to run spends the group's time on a history none of the other six can influence.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to rule on the pilot site so that the meeting can move on to the remaining items.
options.rationale: It hands away the chairing role in the middle of the meeting and rewards the two directors for making the decision uncomfortable to take.

options.text: Adjourn the item and bring the two directors back together separately once tempers have settled.
options.rationale: It removes the heat and the decision together, and the one thing that had to be settled today now needs a further meeting of people who are hard to convene.

options.text: Bring the room back to the pilot site, state the criteria, and ask each director for a position against them.
options.rationale: Re-anchoring on the criteria is what a chair holds authority to do, and it separates today's decision from a dispute that is not on the agenda.

questions.explanation: Chairing carries authority over process rather than over content, and the moment an old grievance enters a decision, the process is exactly what has been lost. Returning the discussion to the stated criteria lets both parties argue fully on the point that matters and leaves the older dispute where it belongs, which is not in front of six uninvolved people. Seniority does not exempt a participant from the rules of the meeting.
questions.mindset: A chair's authority is over how the room decides, and using it is not the same as taking a side.

questions.stem: Your offshore supplier's team has agreed to every date you have proposed for six months. You now learn that the March integration date was never achievable and that their lead knew it in January. He tells you, carefully, that declining a customer's proposal in front of others is not something his team would do. Two further dates have been agreed the same way. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Tell the supplier's lead that commitments have to be honest and that dates will be tracked from now on.
options.rationale: It asks him to behave in a way his own setting penalises, and tracking measures the dates without changing the mechanism that produced them.

options.text: Change how dates are set, so that the supplier proposes them rather than responding to yours.
options.rationale: Proposing a date carries no refusal, so it removes the act he cannot perform while still producing the commitment the project needs.

options.text: Escalate to the supplier's account director that the January date was known to be unachievable.
options.rationale: It makes a contractual matter of a communication norm and costs you the candour of the one person who has now told you the truth.

options.text: Ask the supplier to confirm all remaining dates in writing so that the commitments are unambiguous.
options.rationale: The commitments were never ambiguous; they were given in a setting where disagreement was not available. Written confirmation reproduces them more formally.

options.text: Re-test the two dates already agreed with the lead privately, away from the group setting.
options.rationale: The two live dates are the immediate exposure, and asking in private gives him a context in which a different answer is possible to give.

questions.explanation: A commitment is only as good as the other party's ability to decline, and where the setting makes refusal costly the agreement you receive tells you nothing. The fix is to change your own process so that dissent is available at low cost — different people, different channel, or a question put the other way round — rather than to ask someone to bear a cost you have designed into the meeting. Treating the norm as bad faith destroys the only channel that has started working.
questions.mindset: If saying no is expensive where you asked, the yes you received was not information.

questions.stem: The board pack is issued tomorrow morning. Your benefits analyst puts the programme's annual savings at £2.4 million; the finance business partner's paper puts the same savings at £1.6 million. Each says the other has used the wrong baseline, and both figures have circulated this week. The board chair has already seen the higher one. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Get the two of them to reconcile the difference down to its cause before the pack is issued.
options.rationale: Two figures from one baseline dispute differ for a findable reason, and the reconciliation is a day's work that settles the number rather than the argument.

options.text: Present both figures in the pack and let the board decide which basis it prefers to rely on.
options.rationale: It passes an unresolved technical difference to the people with the least context to settle it, and invites a choice of number rather than of method.

options.text: Use the finance partner's figure, on the basis that finance owns the organisation's reporting standards.
options.rationale: Owning the standard is not the same as having applied it correctly here, and resolving by authority may publish the wrong number with finance's name on it.

options.text: Tell the chair tonight that the number he has seen is in question and when it will be settled.
options.rationale: He is carrying a figure he may repeat, and hearing it from the project manager first is the difference between a correction and a surprise.

options.text: Take the savings figure out of the pack until the two of them have agreed on the method to use.
options.rationale: It removes the item the board most needs in order to govern, and an unexplained omission invites exactly the questions the reconciliation would answer.

questions.explanation: A disagreement between two analysts is a technical question until it reaches a governance forum, at which point it becomes a credibility problem for whoever let it arrive unresolved. The work is to find the cause of the difference rather than to choose between the numbers, and to warn anyone already relying on one of them before they act on it. Publishing both, or neither, moves the conflict into the room least equipped to resolve it.
questions.mindset: Reconcile two numbers to their cause before anyone has to choose between them.

questions.stem: The scheduling supervisor at your client is the only person blocking sign-off of the new planning tool, raising a fresh quality concern each week. Her team of four does manually what the tool will do automatically, and she has twice asked what happens to them. Each of her concerns has been answered on its merits. Go-live is five weeks away. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Obtain sign-off through her manager, since each of her concerns has already been answered properly.
options.rationale: It gets the signature and leaves the person who runs the process opposed to the tool, which is where the next five weeks of quality concerns will come from.

options.text: Reduce the tool's automation so that her team keeps the scheduling work it does today.
options.rationale: It gives away the benefit the client is paying for in order to end the resistance, which resolves the conflict by abandoning the objective.

options.text: Press the client to answer, in writing, what happens to the four roles at go-live.
options.rationale: The unanswered question is what is driving the weekly concerns, and only the client can answer it; the project manager can insist that somebody does.

options.text: Offer her a defined role in the cutover so that her knowledge is visibly needed.
options.rationale: It gives her a stake in the transition rather than a reason to fear it, and her process knowledge is genuinely the scarcest thing available in five weeks.

options.text: Ask your sponsor to escalate the delay to the client's director as a governance issue.
options.rationale: It labels her an obstacle in front of her own leadership while leaving the question about her team unanswered, which tends to harden the resistance.

questions.explanation: Sustained objections that survive being answered are rarely about the stated objections, and the reliable tell is a question the person keeps asking that nobody has addressed. Resolving that conflict means getting the real question answered by whoever owns it, and giving the person a role in what is coming so that the change is not purely something happening to them. Neither surrendering the benefit nor overruling the individual touches the cause.
questions.mindset: When answered objections keep returning, find the question nobody has answered.

questions.stem: Your lead structural engineer and your lead architect are both excellent, and they have been unable to work together for eight months. Two mediations have each held for about a fortnight. Their teams now route everything through deputies, which works, at a cost of roughly a day a week in duplicated review. Neither will move to another project, and both are needed until the design freeze in seven months.

options.text: Run a third mediation, this time with a professional facilitator brought in from outside the organisation entirely.
options.rationale: Two attempts have each decayed within a fortnight, so a third is a bet that the method was the problem rather than the relationship's capacity to hold an agreement.

options.text: Formalise the deputy route as the working arrangement and put the day a week into the plan.
options.rationale: The workaround the teams built is already the thing that works, and making it official converts an unmanaged cost into a planned one.

options.text: Ask the design director to require the two leads to hold a joint design review every week from now on.
options.rationale: It mandates the contact that has twice failed, and a required weekly meeting between two people who cannot work together will be attended rather than used.

options.text: Escalate to the design director as a performance matter concerning both of the individuals.
options.rationale: It turns a working-relationship problem into a conduct case against two people you need for seven months, and neither is failing at their actual work.

questions.explanation: Not every conflict can be resolved, and a project manager's responsibility is to the work rather than to the reconciliation. Where repeated attempts have failed and the parties are both necessary, the right move is often to design the interaction out — through intermediaries, artefacts or sequencing — and to carry the cost openly in the plan rather than to keep paying it invisibly. What makes this legitimate rather than defeatist is that the cost is named, priced and owned.
questions.mindset: Some conflicts are routed around rather than resolved; the discipline is to price the detour and put it in the plan.

questions.stem: The commercial director has told your squad that its estimates are padded and that she expects next quarter's plan to fit into half the time. The squad's last four quarters each landed within ten per cent of forecast. Two developers have said they will not put their names to halved numbers. The quarterly plan is due on Friday.

options.text: Halve the estimates as instructed and record the resulting delivery risk in the programme risk register.
options.rationale: It complies with a number nobody believes and documents the failure in advance, which protects the project manager and no one else on the squad.

options.text: Hold the squad's numbers and ask the sponsor to overrule the commercial director this week.
options.rationale: It turns a question that four quarters of evidence could settle into a contest between two managers, and the squad's forecasts become the prize.

options.text: Show her the four quarters of forecast accuracy and ask what she needs delivered sooner.
options.rationale: The evidence answers the padding claim, and the second question surfaces the commercial pressure that the instruction about estimates was standing in for.

options.text: Offer to re-estimate the next quarter with her in the room, so she can see how the numbers are built.
options.rationale: It treats the estimation method as the objection. She is unlikely to be arguing about technique, and a transparent process will reach the same numbers.

questions.explanation: An instruction to change an estimate is almost never a claim about estimating; it is a date or a commitment arriving in the wrong currency. Answering the stated claim with evidence closes it, and asking what is actually needed moves the conversation to the thing that can be negotiated, which is scope and sequence rather than the numbers themselves. Complying with an estimate you do not believe transfers the risk to the people who have to deliver it.
questions.mindset: Treat pressure on an estimate as a question about the date behind it.

questions.stem: Your programme's dispute protocol says that a disagreement between workstreams is raised with both leads on the day it arises, escalated to the programme manager if it is still unresolved five working days later, and escalated to the sponsor if it is unresolved for a further ten working days after that. A disagreement about interface testing was raised with both leads on Monday 2 March and is still unresolved today.

blanks.label: Working days after 2 March at which the sponsor becomes involved
blanks.rationale: Five working days to the first escalation and ten more beyond it gives fifteen working days in total, which is three calendar weeks rather than fifteen days on the calendar.

blanks.label: Who holds the disagreement between the two escalation points
blanks.rationale: The middle window belongs to the programme manager, whose job during it is to resolve the disagreement rather than to observe it moving towards the sponsor.

blanks.label: What the protocol requires on day one, before any escalation is available
accept: raising it with the two leads
blanks.rationale: Nothing escalates until both leads have been told there is a disagreement, which stops a party reaching a higher level with a dispute the other side has never heard.

questions.explanation: An escalation protocol is a clock as much as a ladder, and its value lies in the fact that both parties know when the disagreement leaves them. The first step matters most: escalation from a position the other side has never been given a chance to answer is what turns a disagreement into a grievance. Working days and calendar days diverge quickly over three weeks, which is why the protocol counts in the unit it does.
questions.mindset: Escalate on the protocol's clock, and never to a level the other party does not yet know the dispute has reached.

questions.stem: The chart tracks one disagreement between your test manager and your release manager across four months, with what each was saying at the four marked points. Select the point at which the disagreement stopped being about the work and became about the two of them.

graphic.title: Rising conflict intensity across four months with a quotation at each marked point
graphic.caption: Select a point. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between points, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: March: we need two more days of regression before each release
