regions.rationale: This is a request about the work with a quantity attached to it, which is the cheapest form a disagreement ever takes and the easiest to test against evidence.

regions.label: April: releases keep getting cut short because testing is being squeezed
regions.rationale: The claim has widened from one release to a pattern, which raises the stakes, but it is still an argument about how the release process runs.

regions.label: May: he has never accepted that testing is not optional
regions.rationale: The subject has moved from the process to the other person's standing beliefs, and a claim about what someone has never accepted cannot be settled by any change to the release schedule.

regions.label: June: both managers copy their directors on every message
regions.rationale: Copying in directors is a consequence of a dispute that had already become personal, so treating this as the turning point puts the intervention a month too late.

questions.explanation: Disagreements about the work are settled with evidence, timing or a decision; disagreements about a person are not, and the same remedy applied after the shift achieves nothing. The turn is usually visible in the language, when specific claims about an event give way to general claims about what someone always or never does. Spotting it matters because the interventions available before the shift are far cheaper than the ones needed after it.
questions.mindset: Watch for the moment the language turns from what happened to what someone always does.

questions.stem: A long-running disagreement between your squad and the security function has produced three separate questions. Match each to the place it should be settled. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Whether the squad may ship with its current logging design, which the security lead says falls short of the standard.
Whether a two-day turnaround on security reviews is realistic, given that the security team covers eleven squads.
Whether the squad and the security team keep missing each other's sessions because neither books the other in.

options.text: With the owner of the security standard, who can interpret it or grant a documented exception.
options.rationale: Whether a design meets a standard is a question about the standard, and only its owner can say so or record a departure from it that will survive audit.

options.text: With the sponsor, as a question about funding the capacity that the turnaround implies.
options.rationale: A turnaround commitment across eleven squads is a capacity decision with a price, and neither the squad nor the security lead controls that budget.

options.text: At the change control board, as a proposed change to an approved project baseline.
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three is a change to something already agreed: two are questions about a standard and its resourcing, and the third is a working habit.

options.text: Between the two leads, as a working agreement about how reviews are booked and returned.
options.rationale: Missed sessions are a matter of habit between two teams, and the people who can change it are the ones who run the calendars, not anyone above them.

questions.explanation: A single long-running conflict usually contains several different questions, and it persists because they are argued together in one forum that can only answer one of them. Separating them lets each go to whoever has the standing to settle it: policy questions to the policy owner, capacity questions to whoever funds capacity, and habits to the people with the habit. Escalating the bundle guarantees an answer to the wrong question.
questions.mindset: Split a stuck conflict into its separate questions before deciding where any of it should go.

questions.stem: During your depot rollout the operations director has taken three positions in the same negotiation. Match each to the underlying interest it most likely reflects. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: We cannot take the new handheld terminals into any depot before September.
Your training has to be delivered by our own supervisors, not by anyone from your team.
We want the pilot depot to be Warrington rather than Crewe.

options.text: Protecting the summer peak, during which the depots cannot absorb any disruption at all.
options.rationale: A date expressed as the earliest acceptable one usually protects the period before it, and for a depot network the summer peak is the obvious thing being shielded.

options.text: Preserving the supervisors' standing with crews who take instruction from them and not from visitors.
options.rationale: Insisting on who delivers rather than on what is delivered points at authority rather than content, and supervisors lose standing when someone else teaches their crews.

options.text: Avoiding the site where the last system rollout went badly and the crews still remember it.
options.rationale: A preference between two similar sites is rarely about the sites, and a depot carrying a bad memory of a previous rollout is a poor place to prove a new one.

options.text: Reducing the total cost of the rollout as it falls on the operations budget.
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three positions moves money: later delivery, local trainers and a different pilot site are broadly cost-neutral to the operations budget.

questions.explanation: A position is what someone asks for; an interest is what they are protecting, and only the second one can be traded against something else. Positions that look unreasonable usually become negotiable the moment the interest behind them is named, because there is often more than one way to protect it. The work is to ask what each demand is guarding rather than to argue with the demand as stated.
questions.mindset: Ask what a demand is protecting, because interests have alternatives and positions do not.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: You settle a disagreement about test scope in a meeting, then email the same group that evening reopening the point you conceded. This would
You raise a disagreement between two workstream leads with both of their line managers before either lead has been told there is a problem. This would

options.text: give both parties a written record of the disagreement that they can rely on later
options.rationale: Not used. Neither sentence describes a situation a record would improve: the first is a reopened agreement and the second is an escalation nobody has been warned about.

options.text: teach the group that agreements reached in the room hold only until you have slept on them
options.rationale: Reopening a concession after the meeting means nothing agreed in a meeting can be relied on, and people start negotiating for the written round instead of the spoken one.

options.text: turn a disagreement into a performance matter for two people who were never given the chance to settle it
options.rationale: Going to line managers first puts both leads in front of the people who write their appraisals, which changes what the disagreement is about for everyone involved.

questions.explanation: Most of the damage a project manager does in a conflict comes from how the conflict is handled rather than from the decision reached. Two habits do most of it: reopening settled points outside the setting where they were settled, which makes agreement worthless, and escalating to a level that carries consequences for someone before they know there is anything to answer. Both are about predictability, which is the thing that makes people willing to settle at all.
questions.mindset: Handle a disagreement so that people can predict what you will do with it; that predictability is what makes agreement possible.
